source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025)
finding: Dynamic benchmark. 1,000 auto-generated questions about unresolved future events, from nine sources (markets and datasets), refreshed nightly. No leakage by construction.
numbers: 9 sources; question bank updated 0:00 UTC nightly; question sets released every 2 weeks; 17 LLMs in the initial set; Brier score, 0.25 = always say 50%.
quote: To avoid any possibility of data leakage, ForecastBench is comprised solely of questions about future events that have no known answer
limits: Dataset questions are templated; market questions favour topics with liquid markets.
agent_relevance: Gives a leak-free test for any scaffold we build: score only on questions that have no answer yet.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - human baselines
finding: Two human groups were surveyed on a random 200-question subset: 500 public participants and 39 superforecasters. Each group is scored by its per-question median.
numbers: Public: 500 people via Prolific/Facebook, at least 40 forecasts per question, mean 49. Superforecasters: 39, 9-day study, min 3 forecasts per question, mean 8; they saw each other's forecasts and rationales halfway through.
limits: Superforecaster median is a small-group, partly deliberated aggregate. Human groups last surveyed July 2024 (leaderboard note), so the human line is fixed while LLMs move.
agent_relevance: The target is a deliberating small-team median, not a lone person. A multi-attempt scaffold with discussion is the fair analogue.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - headline result (Table 2)
finding: On the 200-question human subset, superforecasters beat both the public and the best LLM. The best LLM only matched the public median.
numbers: Superforecasters Brier 0.096; general public 0.121 (p<0.001 vs supers); best LLM Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.122 (scratchpad + freeze values), p<0.001 vs supers. Best LLM without crowd forecast on market questions: 0.136.
limits: Best LLMs were given the market crowd forecast (freeze value), so part of their skill is copying the crowd. Bootstrapped p-values.
agent_relevance: Without the crowd anchor the gap is bigger (0.136 vs 0.096). Score an agent with and without any anchor it is handed.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - seven baselines
finding: Seven LLM baselines: zero-shot, scratchpad, scratchpad+news, each with or without freeze values, plus a 9-forecast ensemble (3 models x 3 superforecaster-written prompts).
numbers: Ensemble aggregations on the model-selection set: median 0.197, trimmed mean 0.197, geometric mean 0.194, geometric mean of log odds 0.194 (2 SE about 0.024; Table 17). Best single-model scratchpad there: Claude 3.5 Sonnet 0.178 (Table 16).
limits: Aggregation rules differ by only 0.003; ensemble gain over best single model is small in this table.
agent_relevance: Aggregation formula matters little; the gap comes from information and reasoning, not averaging.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - combination questions
finding: LLMs are much worse on combination questions (conjunctions/disjunctions of two base questions). Including them widens the gap to humans.
numbers: Including combo questions: superforecasters 0.076, public 0.096, GPT-4o 0.130. Gap 0.054, bigger than the 0.026 gap between GPT-4o and GPT-4. Human combo scores assume independence of the parts.
limits: Human combo numbers are constructed, not elicited (lower bound on human skill).
agent_relevance: Consistency over linked questions is a weak spot; a code-side coherence check (G5) targets it.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - category and horizon breakdown (Tables 25-26)
finding: Best LLM nearly ties or wins in some slices. Superforecasters win most slices.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet vs supers: Economics & Business (N=181) 0.126 vs 0.141 (LLM better); 7-day horizon (N=106) 0.093 vs 0.076 (gap 0.017); 30-day (N=112) 0.151 vs 0.172 (LLM better). Text says LLM also better at 90 days.
limits: Small N per cell; the PDF text layer scrambles some rows, so only clearly aligned cells are quoted.
agent_relevance: The gap is not uniform; per-category gaps show where a scaffold may already be at parity.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: a dynamic benchmark of AI forecasting capabilities (ICLR 2025) - extrapolation to parity
finding: Brier falls linearly with Chatbot Arena score and with log training compute. Extrapolated, LLMs reach superforecaster level at Arena about 1406 or compute about 6.5e26 FLOP.
numbers: Arena fit: Brier = 0.506 - 0.000298 x Arena, R2 = 0.47; match at 1406 (95% CI 1346-1633). Compute fit: Brier = 0.844 - 0.01213 x log10(compute), R2 = 0.41, r = -0.67, p = 0.046; match at 6.49e26 (95% CI 9.69e25 to 8.65e28).
limits: Very wide intervals; 17 models; marginal significance; assumes linearity. The 'parity around November 2026' date is NOT in this paper; it comes from the FRI site/index row.
agent_relevance: Scaling alone predicts parity; we test whether a scaffold closes the gap at fixed model size.

source: ForecastBench leaderboard site (FRI), fetched 2026-11-01
finding: Leaderboard has Tournament (scaffolds, fine-tuning, ensembles allowed), Preliminary and Baseline (base models, no tools) tabs. Ranking is by Overall Brier Index, the equal-weight mean of dataset and market difficulty-adjusted Brier scores. Models appear 50 days after submission. Human groups last surveyed July 2024.
numbers: Table rows were not in the fetched text, so the current 0.017 gap and the November 2026 parity projection could NOT be verified here.
limits: Difficulty adjustment means current scores are not on the same scale as the 2024 paper's raw Brier numbers.
agent_relevance: Report our scaffold on the Tournament and Baseline tracks separately; they answer different questions.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models
finding: Retrieval-augmented system (query decomposition, news relevance filtering, scratchpad reasoning, fine-tuned reasoner, trimmed-mean ensemble) comes near the crowd aggregate on post-cutoff questions.
numbers: 5,516 binary questions from 5 platforms: 3,762 train, 840 validation, 914 test (all opened after 1 June 2023). Test Brier: system 0.179, crowd 0.149, system+crowd average 0.146. Best zero-shot base model GPT-4-1106 0.208; random 0.25.
quote: None of the models are naturally good at forecasting. Most models' scores are around or worse than random guessing
limits: System loses to the crowd overall; beats it only in a selective setting (crowd uncertain 0.3-0.7, early retrieval, 5+ relevant articles). Paleka et al. (2025) find at least 3.8% of questions resolved early.
agent_relevance: Averaging model and crowd beats both. A scaffold gains most when evidence is rich and the crowd is unsure; retrieval depth is a gate.

source: Halawi et al. (2024) - fine-tuning and aggregation details
finding: Self-supervised fine-tune: sample many reasonings, keep those whose forecast beat the crowd, fine-tune on them. Final forecast is a trimmed mean of base and fine-tuned runs. Prompt tells the model to hedge less and use base rates.
numbers: Final ensemble 6 forecasts (3 base, 3 fine-tuned); temperature 0.5 for the fine-tuned model; hyperparameters chosen on validation only.
limits: GPT-4-class models; whether the gain survives newer reasoning models is open.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot fine-tune, but can select outcomes against a reference in-session.

source: Zou et al. (2022) Forecasting future world events with neural networks (Autocast)
finding: Founding static benchmark for ML forecasting: questions from Metaculus, Good Judgment Open and CSET, plus a date-sorted news corpus to simulate the past. Models far below the crowd.
numbers: Best ML model 65% accuracy on true/false vs 92% for the human crowd (random 50%). Calibration error: largest FiD Static model 40%, human crowd 8%, FiD Temporal 17%. Retrieval gave relative gains of 93% over UnifiedQA-v2 and 15% over T5.
limits: 2022 models (T5/GPT-2 scale); retrodiction design has leakage risks (Paleka 2025).
agent_relevance: Start of the line. 40% vs 8% calibration error is the older form of today's hedging/overconfidence problem.

source: Schoenegger & Park (2023) LLM prediction capabilities: evidence from a real-world forecasting tournament
finding: GPT-4 entered a 3-month Metaculus tournament (Jul-Oct 2023, 843 participants) and was not better than guessing 50%.
numbers: N = 23 resolved binary questions. GPT-4 Brier 0.20 (SD 0.18); human crowd median 0.07 (SD 0.08). GPT-4 vs 0.25 baseline: t(22) = -1.23, p = 0.23. Crowd vs baseline: t(22) = -10.69, p < .001.
limits: Tiny N (23); one model; superforecaster-persona prompt. Hypothesis that GPT-4 hugs 50% was not supported.
agent_relevance: A 2023 model could not beat a constant 0.5. Sets the floor.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd (Study 1)
finding: Median of 12 LLMs was not statistically different from 925 human forecasters. Preregistered null; exploratory equivalence test passed with wide bounds.
numbers: 31 binary questions. LLM crowd mean Brier 0.20 (SD 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Equivalence at Cohen d=0.5 (0.081 Brier): lower p=0.017, upper p=0.040. Single models: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4+Bing 0.16, Claude 2 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38.
limits: Only 31 questions: low power (Bench to the Future says so). Wide bounds. Human comparison was not superforecasters. Acquiescence: mean model forecasts above 50% while just over 45% resolved yes.
agent_relevance: Median over diverse models works, but our G4 says one model's samples are not independent; this crowd used 12 different models. Add a yes-bias correction.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: LLMs shown the human median
finding: Showing GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human crowd median improved them, but averaging model and human forecasts was better still.
numbers: 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts per model over the 31 questions. GPT-4 Brier 0.17 -> 0.14 (p=0.003). Claude 2 0.22 -> 0.15 (p<0.001). Gains of 17% to 28%.
limits: Model moves toward the anchor, so part of the gain is copying.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as ForecastBench freeze values. Averaging in code beats asking the model to update.

source: Pratt et al. (2024) Can language models use forecasting strategies?
finding: Dataset of real events with human prediction series (over 1,000 humans per split, median about 100 predictions). LLM forecasters struggle; a main confound is a tendency to guess events will not happen.
numbers: Introduces a Weighted Brier Score that scores resolved-yes and resolved-no events separately, so 'always say unlikely' cannot look good.
limits: Largely negative results; short horizon; platform-specific.
agent_relevance: Report accuracy split by outcome class.

source: Hsieh, Fu, Chen (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Forecasting (RTF)
finding: ReAct agents with search and a Python tool for numeric simulation; agent ensembles match the human crowd and beat base LMs.
numbers: RTF mean of 3: Brier 0.170 (73.9% accuracy); human crowd 0.172 (73.8%); RTF single sampled 0.180; Halawi pipeline on GPT-4o 0.177; base GPT-4o 0.210; base LM mean 0.218. Ensembling helped agents (0.169 vs 0.180) but not base LMs (0.218 vs 0.210).
limits: Two-week-horizon questions; Google date filter used against leakage (see Paleka 2025).
agent_relevance: Tools plus simulation helped; ensembling pays when members differ in process.

source: Lu (2025) Evaluating LLMs on real-world forecasting against expert forecasters
finding: On 464 Metaculus questions (two quarters), frontier models passed the 2024 human-crowd Brier but lost clearly to Metaculus-hired experts on the subset they forecast.
numbers: o3 Brier 0.1352 (better than Halawi crowd 0.149, worse than ForecastBench public 0.121); o3-pro 0.1307 on a smaller subset; GPT-4.1 0.1542; o4-mini 0.1589; GPT-4-1106 about 0.20; GPT-4o-mini 0.2743. Ten experts, 157 questions: median Brier 0.0225, mean 0.1573 (SE 0.0189). Naive linear extrapolation: superforecaster level before May 2027.
limits: Expert median (0.0225) far below mean (0.157): a few big misses; experts predicted only 47% of bot-days. Brier is not comparable across question sets.
agent_relevance: Median-vs-mean gap warns that headline expert numbers hide tails. Report both.

source: Lu (2025) vs Karger (2025): two parity forecasts
finding: Two independent linear extrapolations give different parity dates: ForecastBench Arena/compute fits (CI very wide) and Lu's release-date fit (before May 2027).
numbers: Karger: Arena 1406 (CI 1346-1633). Lu: frontier Brier vs release date, naive linear, 'before May 2027'.
limits: Both linear on few points; neither includes scaffolds.
agent_relevance: Parity date is not a reliable planning number.

source: Paleka, Goel, Geiping, Tramer (2025) Pitfalls in evaluating language model forecasters
finding: Two classes of problem: temporal leakage in backtests, and weak link between benchmark score and real forecasting skill. Date-restricted search often leaks.
numbers: At least 3.8% of Halawi et al. questions resolved early (no forecast needed). In Tao et al. at least 10% trivial. Auto-generated news questions (Dai et al.) let weak classifiers reach over 80% accuracy. Search engines return post-cutoff pages despite date filters.
quote: Claims that LLMs 'match human performance' may then be circular
limits: Mostly case examples and estimates; authors say some leaks cannot be confirmed.
agent_relevance: Prefer live (ForecastBench) over backtest numbers; if backtesting, use a frozen offline corpus.

source: Paleka et al. (2025) Consistency checks for language model forecasters
finding: Measures forecaster logical consistency (negation, conditionals, etc.) as arbitrage profit; instant consistency correlates with later Brier score.
numbers: 2,621 ground-truth resolved questions in the benchmark. Correlation of consistency violation with Brier up to 0.92 for one check on scraped questions (aggregate frequentist metric 0.85) and 0.49-0.69 on the other set; some checks give little signal.
limits: Modest number of forecasters; models worse than 0.25 excluded; Brier depends on knowledge cutoff.
agent_relevance: Cheap, instant, code-computed check usable inside the agent (G5): enforce P(A)+P(not A)=1 and conditional chains.

source: Turtel, Franklin, Skotheim, Hewitt, Schoenegger (2025) Outcome-based RL to predict the future
finding: RL on resolved Polymarket questions made a 14B model match o1 on Brier and calibrate better. No model beat Polymarket's own price.
numbers: 1,265 held-out questions. 7-run ReMax ensemble Brier 0.190 [0.178,0.203], ECE 0.062; Modified-GRPO 0.192, ECE 0.054; o1 0.202, ECE 0.093. Simulated trading ROI above 10%. Plain GRPO drifted to overconfidence or collapse.
limits: Training on market data; market price still better; ROI is a simulation.
agent_relevance: Training fixed calibration (ECE 0.062 vs 0.093); a scaffold must fix it in code.

source: FutureSearch (2025) Bench to the Future: a pastcasting benchmark
finding: Pastcasting: already-resolved questions with an offline corpus of tens of thousands of pages. Shows steady model progress; says the silicon-crowd study lacked power.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 3.5 (original) 0.1925, 3.7 0.1712, 3.5v2 0.1690, 3.7 thinking 0.1645, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.1611, Sonnet 4 thinking 0.1597, Sonnet 4 0.1560. Pairwise p for Sonnet 3.7 vs 4: 0.139, so neighbours are often not distinguishable. Effective question count 178.8 after correlation weighting.
limits: Corpus may hold hints; no human baseline; model memory still possible.
agent_relevance: A repeatable offline test bed for scaffold ablations without waiting for resolution.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster technical report
finding: Agentic search + supervisor agent reconciling forecasts + statistical calibration (Platt scaling, i.e. extremizing) reaches superforecaster parity on ForecastBench snapshots.
numbers: Brier: FB-7-21 AIA 0.1076 vs supers 0.1110, public 0.1451, o3 0.133; FB-8-14 supers 0.1152, public 0.1510, prior best LLM 0.145; FB-Market AIA 0.0753 vs supers 0.0740, market 0.0965. MarketLiquid: AIA 0.1258 vs market 0.1106 (loses); AIA+market ensemble beats market.
quote: On this benchmark, the AIA Forecaster is statistically indistinguishable from superforecasters
limits: Indistinguishable, not better. Authors call ForecastBench relatively easy. Company report, not peer reviewed. Extremizing here corrects one forecast for RLHF hedging; our G4 bans extremizing votes, a different operation, but check calibration is fitted on held-out data.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a scaffold, not training, can close the 2024 gap.

source: Alur et al. (2025) AIA Forecaster - ablations
finding: Search quality changes Brier a little on ForecastBench. Market price as input gives large gains on market questions.
numbers: No search 0.1230; non-agentic Search-B 0.12168; agentic Search-B 0.11824; non-agentic Search-A 0.11738; agentic Search-A 0.1140. Market subset: LLM no search 0.116; with market price 0.103 (11.2% better); market price alone 0.096; agentic search 0.085; agentic search + market price 0.075 (11.8% better). Per-event median beats mean: supers 0.1110 vs 0.1123, public 0.1450 vs 0.1586.
limits: Poor search is about as good as none.
agent_relevance: Search helps only with good sources. LLMs hedge toward 0.5 after RLHF; extremizing corrects it.

source: Cross-paper check: public-median Brier varies by question set
finding: The same public-survey group has Brier 0.121 (ForecastBench 200-subset, paper), 0.1451 (FB-7-21, AIA recomputation), 0.1510 (FB-8-14).
numbers: Differences come from question subset and which horizons/combos are included.
limits: Do not mix absolute Brier across papers.
agent_relevance: Use paired comparisons on the same questions.

source: Project index row (SUBFIELDS.md) on ForecastBench gap
finding: Index row says: experts beat the top LLM (p<0.001); gap to superforecasters now 0.017 Brier, about one year of LLM progress; parity projected around November 2026 with a wide interval.
numbers: 0.017 gap and Nov 2026 date: not verified (leaderboard tables not retrievable; web search budget exhausted). Note the 7-day-horizon gap in the 2025 paper is also 0.017 (0.093 vs 0.076), possibly a mix-up.
limits: May be a difficulty-adjusted metric rather than raw Brier.
agent_relevance: Re-fetch the live leaderboard or GitHub datasets before quoting these numbers.
